the neural mechanisms of breathing and in particular with the control of breathing by the brain stem.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the PSRs do not play a major role in the genesis of the inspiratory activity during the ventilatory cycles without inflation.
the inspiratory activity of paralyzed, ventilated, vagotomized animals is greater during the second ventilatory cycle without lung inflation than during the previous cycle.
the responses recorded from phrenic and hypo-glossal nerves during the second cycle of ventilation without inflation are not attributable to the frequency of discharge from PSRs.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the inspiratory activity of the cat is determined by a balance of excitatory and inhibitory influences from lung inflation, and from the central nervous system.
the inspiratory response to lung inflation is not only a function of lung volume but also of the duration of inflation.
, during normal ventilation, PSRs are activated during lung inflation and inhibit motor output.
The main takeaway from our work is that
PSR discharge is not a simple reflection of lung inflation but rather is a dynamic process that is influenced by a variety of factors.
lung inflation can have an effect on the brain that outlasts the actual inflation.
the activity of PSRs is not only dependent on lung inflation but also on the absence of lung inflation.
